data.name: PD-1/PD-L1
data.comments:
• PD-1/PD-L1 test protocol

  • Cell ratio 1:1 --> Jurkat PD-1 Effector cells cocultures with CHO-PD-L1 aAPC/CHO-K1 (140.000 cells of each).

  • Antibody dilutions 1/2. First point 2-4 ug/ml (10 dilutions).

 

  • Day 0: seed 140.000 CHO-PD-L1 aAPC/CHO-K1/well in DMEM 10%FBS in a 96-well flat white plate.

  • Day 1:

  • +Remove DMEM carefully. 

+ Add 140.000 Jurkat PD-1 cells/well (in 40ul of RPMI 1%FBS)

+ Add the antibody dilutions in 40 µl of RPMI (prepare each dilution of antibody in 40ul, but taking in count that the final volume will be 80ul).

+ Incubate 6 hours at 37ºC.

+ After incubation, add 80ul/well of BioGlo Reagent and measure luminescence.

  • Data are presented as fold of induction relative to the values obtained from unblocked Jurkat PD-1 Cells co-cultured with CHO-PD-L1 aAPC/CHO-K1 (no antibody). 


Defrost cells CHO-PD-L1 and Jurkat-PD1 cells and plate each of them in a petri dish. Use  20 ml of DMEM + 10% FBS + 1% antibiotics (strept/pen) for CHO-PD-L1 and RPMI 1640 + 1% antibiotics (strept/pen) for Jurkat-PD1.
After a few days check if a reasonable amount of cells are present for both  CHO-PD-L1 and Jurkat-PD1. If yes, prepare the peptide labelling it with Alexa-488 and plate 140000 cells in each well of a white 96-well plates.

data.name: Time Laps QBP1-Alexa488
data.comments:
Alexa488 conjugation Assay Procedure 
Ensure all materials and prepared reagents are equilibrated to room temperature prior to use. 
Add Modifier: Add 1 µL of Modifier reagent for every 10 µL of antibody to be labeled, then mix gently (10 ul for a sample of 100 ul). 
Combine Reagents: Remove the cap from the Alexa Fluor® 488 Conjugation Mix vial. Pipette the antibody sample (now containing the Modifier) directly onto the lyophilized material. Resuspend gently by pipetting the liquid up and down once or twice.
Incubate: Replace the cap on the vial and let it stand in the dark at room temperature (20-25°C) for 15 minutes. Note: Longer incubation times, such as overnight, will not negatively impact the conjugation process. 
Quench: After incubating for at least 15 minutes, add 1 µL of Quencher reagent for every 10 µL of initial antibody used, and mix gently (10 ul for a sample of 100 ul). The conjugate is ready to use after 5 minutes and does not require any purification steps.

We treated 100 ul of QBP1 100 uM with 10 ul if modifier and 10 of quencher.

After seeding 8000 cells of the two cell lines in DMEM +10 FBS + 1% antibiotics (Strept/pen) on day 0 (80 ul per well), we stained teh cells for microscopy after one day.

                                                                                                                                                          Staining protocol for microscopy

About the staining mother solutions:
  • Hoescht: stock at 10 mg/ml
  • DRAQ7: 1uM (stock at 0.1 mM)
  • WGA-555: 5ug/ml (stock at 1 mg/ml)

WGA-555 was added to the medium at a concentration of 5 ng/ml. This dye should localize on the membrane. After one hour we removed the medium and washed with PBS. We added fresh medium (50 ul, which is the minimum not to waster dye) and we stained with the following dyes (we might have done all at the dyes at once but care must be taken as WGA-555 might bind to glycoproteins of FBS).
To visualize nuclei we need to use low concentration of Hoescht (1 ng per well but better 0.5 ng) to avoid toxicity. The dye is dissolved in the medium (50 ul). The incubation must be between 40 minutes to 1 hour.
We can also add 1 uM DRAQ7 which penetrates the cells only when they are dead. The dye is dissolved in the medium. This incubation can be done at the same time with Hoesch.

Check with the microscope if staining has worked before adding the peptide and setup the microscope for timelaps.
We added the peptide (we removed 25 ul of the medium out of the 50 and added 25 ul of peptide 100uM) and we ran an analisis of 24 hours with pictures every 2 hours. In the case of the higher dilution 5 ul of peptide were added to the mediul after reving 5 uL of medium.

data.name: Microscopy-Transfection
data.comments:
Transfection protocol for 25 wells of a 96-well plate
1. Seed the plates (Day 1)
​Seed 15 wells with U2OS (1.75 x 10⁴ cells/well) in DMEM + 10%FBS and antibiotics (1% strepto/pen).
​Seed 15 wells with A549 (1.25 x 10⁴ cells/well) in DMEM + 10%FBS and antibiotics (1% strepto/pen).
​Use 100 µL of complete media per well.
​No antibiotics.
​Incubate overnight.

In our case we seeded 8000 cells per well with antibiotics but we will not use antibiotics in the following steps. 

​2. Make the shared DNA mix (Day 2)
​In Tube 1 (DNA), mix 3.0 µg of plasmid DNA into 150 µL of Opti-MEM.

In our case we have the following plasmid concentrations:
pIRES2-EGFP (vector) :230 ng/ul
BadH: 180 ng/ul 
BadR:550 ng/ul
P53H:142 ng/ul
P53R:116 ng/ul
Which correspond to the following volume to add:
pIRES2-EGFP: 13 ul
BadH: 17 ul
BadR :5.5 ul
P53H : 21 ul
P53R:116 ng/ul : 26 ul

​3. Make the two Lipofectamine mixes (Day 2)
Mix 7 µL of Lipofectamine 2000 into 125 µL of Opti-MEM (for each plasmid). We call it tube U.
​Wait exactly 5 minutes.

​4. Combine the mixes (Day 2)
​Transfer 125 µL from Tube 1 (DNA) into Tube U.
​Mix both gently and wait 20 minutes.

​5. Transfect and Wash (Day 2)
​Add 10 µL of Tube U to each of the wells where the medium has been replaced with OPTIMEM without antibiotics after removing previous medium and washing with PBS.
​4 to 6 hours later (Critical step): Aspirate the media from all 50 wells and replace it with 100 µL of fresh complete media.

We added 20 ul of Tube U to each of the wells.
We changed the media after 4 hours and we put fresh DMEM + 10% FBS (no antibiotics).
We checked fluorescence after 29 hours.

data.name: Time Laps p53H,MycH-Alexa488
data.comments:
Alexa488 conjugation Assay Procedure 
Ensure all materials and prepared reagents are equilibrated to room temperature prior to use. 
Add Modifier: Add 1 µL of Modifier reagent for every 10 µL of antibody to be labeled, then mix gently (10 ul for a sample of 100 ul). 
Combine Reagents: Remove the cap from the Alexa Fluor® 488 Conjugation Mix vial. Pipette the antibody sample (now containing the Modifier) directly onto the lyophilized material. Resuspend gently by pipetting the liquid up and down once or twice.
Incubate: Replace the cap on the vial and let it stand in the dark at room temperature (20-25°C) for 15 minutes. Note: Longer incubation times, such as overnight, will not negatively impact the conjugation process. 
Quench: After incubating for at least 15 minutes, add 1 µL of Quencher reagent for every 10 µL of initial antibody used, and mix gently (10 ul for a sample of 100 ul). The conjugate is ready to use after 5 minutes and does not require any purification steps.

We treated 100 ul of p53H and MycH 100 uM with 10 ul if modifier and 10 of quencher.

After seeding 8000 cells of the two cell lines in DMEM +10 FBS + 1% antibiotics (Strept/pen) on day 0 (80 ul), we stained teh cells for microscopy after one day.

                                                                                                                                                          Staining protocol for microscopy

About the staining mother solutions:
  • Hoescht: stock at 10 mg/ml
  • DRAQ7: 1uM (stock at 0.1 mM)
  • WGA-555: 5ug/ml (stock at 1 mg/ml)

Before adding dyes we replaeced the media with fresh DMEM without FBS and without antibiotics (50 ul). Wethen  added WGA-555 to the medium at a concentration of 5 ng/ml. This dye should localize on the membrane but we saw it next to teh nucleus. This dye is probably not working well. After one hour we removed the medium and washed with PBS. We added fresh medium with FBS 10% and antibiotics and we stained with the following dyes.
To visualize nuclei we need to use low concentration of Hoescht (1 ng per well but better 0.5 ng, teh value that we used) to avoid toxicity. The dye is dissolved in the medium (50 ul). The incubation must be between 40 minutes to 1 hour (we waited 2 hours). 
We also added 0.3 uM DRAQ7 (we did not have enough to put 1uM) which penetrates the cells only when they are dead. The dye is dissolved in the medium. This incubation can be done at the same time with Hoesch.

Check with the microscope if staining has worked before adding the peptide and setup the microscope for timelaps.
After removing 25 ul of medium, we added the peptide (25 ul of peptide 100 uM) and we ran an analisis of 12 hours with pictures every 30 minutes. In the case of the higher dilution 2.5 ul of peptide were added to teh mediul after reving 2.5 uL of medium.

Ensure all materials and prepared reagents are equilibrated to room temperature prior to use. 
Add Modifier: Add 1 µL of Modifier reagent for every 10 µL of antibody to be labeled, then mix gently (10 ul for a sample of 100 ul). 
Combine Reagents: Remove the cap from the Alexa Fluor® 488 Conjugation Mix vial. Pipette the antibody sample (now containing the Modifier) directly onto the lyophilized material. Resuspend gently by pipetting the liquid up and down once or twice.
Incubate: Replace the cap on the vial and let it stand in the dark at room temperature (20-25°C) for 15 minutes. Note: Longer incubation times, such as overnight, will not negatively impact the conjugation process. 
Quench: After incubating for at least 15 minutes, add 1 µL of Quencher reagent for every 10 µL of initial antibody used, and mix gently (10 ul for a sample of 100 ul). The conjugate is ready to use after 5 minutes and does not require any purification steps.

We treated 100 ul of p53H and MycH 100 uM with 10 ul if modifier and 10 of quencher.

After seeding 8000 cells of the two cell lines in DMEM +10 FBS + 1% antibiotics (Strept/pen) on day 0 (80 ul), we stained teh cells for microscopy after one day.

                                                                                                                                                          Staining protocol for microscopy

About the staining mother solutions:
  • Hoescht: stock at 10 mg/ml
  • DRAQ7: 1uM (stock at 0.1 mM)
  • WGA-555: 5ug/ml (stock at 1 mg/ml)

Before adding dyes we replaeced the media with fresh DMEM without FBS and without antibiotics (50 ul). Wethen  added WGA-555 to the medium at a concentration of 5 ng/ml. This dye should localize on the membrane but we saw it next to teh nucleus. This dye is probably not working well. After one hour we removed the medium and washed with PBS. We added fresh medium with FBS 10% and antibiotics and we stained with the following dyes.
To visualize nuclei we need to use low concentration of Hoescht (1 ng per well but better 0.5 ng, teh value that we used) to avoid toxicity. The dye is dissolved in the medium (50 ul). The incubation must be between 40 minutes to 1 hour (we waited 2 hours). 
We also added 0.3 uM DRAQ7 (we did not have enough to put 1uM) which penetrates the cells only when they are dead. The dye is dissolved in the medium. This incubation can be done at the same time with Hoesch.

Check with the microscope if staining has worked before adding the peptide and setup the microscope for timelaps.
After removing 25 ul of medium, we added the peptide (25 ul of peptide 100 uM) and we ran an analisis of 12 hours with pictures every 30 minutes. In the case of the higher dilution 2.5 ul of peptide were added to teh mediul after reving 2.5 uL of medium.

data.background:
The p53 protein, encoded by the TP53 gene, is a master tumor suppressor and transcription factor that maintains genomic stability against stresses like DNA damage. It can induce cell cycle arrest to pause mitosis and allow DNA repair, or trigger apoptosis under severe stress by transactivating a wide array of target genes. While over 50% of human cancers harbor TP53 mutations, the remainder frequently neutralize wild-type p53 through rapid degradation, aberrant post-translational modifications, or sequestration into inactive complexes-whether with regulatory proteins like Mdm2, Mdmx [1,2,3], and mortalin [4,5], or through dominant-negative interactions with mutant p53 in heterozygous contexts[6,7].

p53 is organized into five critical structural regions [8]. At the N-terminus, the Transactivation Domain (TAD) binds general transcription factors and negative regulators like Mdm2 and Mdmx via a hydrophobic alpha-helix relying on specific residues such as Phe19, Trp23 and Leu26. Adjacent to this is the Proline-Rich Domain (PRD), which provides structural flexibility. The central DNA-Binding Domain (DBD) utilizes a loop-sheet-helix structure for sequence-specific DNA binding. Its stability depends heavily on a tetrahedrally coordinated zinc ion, making this architecture a major hotspot for tumorigenic missense mutations. Toward the C-terminus, the Oligomerization Domain (OD) allows four p53 monomers to assemble into a functional tetrameric holoenzyme. Finally, the C-Terminal Domain (CTD) is a basic region essential for facilitating structure-specific chromatin binding in vivo.

Under normal conditions, p53 is kept at low levels through its interaction with Mdmx (also known as Mdm4) and Mdm2 (also known as Hdm2 in humans), the latter targeting it for ubiquitination and subsequent degradation by the proteasome[2]. Phosphorylation of p53 in response to cellular stress at the level of Thr18, close to the key residue Phe19, disrupts its interaction with Mdm2, leading to p53 stabilization and activation of its downstream pathways, including apoptosis. In many cancers, p53 is mutated or deleted; however, in tumors where p53 is wild-type but functionally inactivated by Mdm2 overexpression, inhibiting the Mdm2-p53 interaction has emerged as a therapeutic strategy to reactivate p53 and induce apoptosis in cancer cells. There is strong evidence that Mdm2-p53 inhibitors like Nutlin-3, MI-219, RG7112, RG7388, SAR405838 can selectively kill cancer cells without harming healthy cells significantly [9]. MI-219 activates p53 and causes complete tumor growth inhibition in xenographs [10]. Nutlin derivatives (like RG7112, RG7388 (idasanutlin), and SAR405838) have entered clinical trials [11]. These inhibitors are small organic molecules which take the place of p53 in the interaction pocket.

A key weakness of small organic molecules as drugs is their susceptibility to point mutations in the target binding pocket, which can weaken drug binding and restore the interaction with the undesired protein partner. In contrast, interfering peptides-designed to mimic the natural protein interface-are less affected by such mutations, as changes that disrupt peptide binding would also impair the native protein-protein interaction. A peptide selected by phage display and similar to a fragment of the transactivation domain of p53 (TSFAEYWNLLSP) showed to interact with Mdm2 (and MdmX) protein with nanomolar affinity in wt p53 human osteosarcoma cell line U2OS, thus inhibiting the p53-MDM2 interaction [12]. The sequence was refined to an improved mutated version (TSFAEYWNLLSP, hereon p53_R) [13]. A further modification of this peptide with β-residues demonstrated to induce apoptosis in U2OS cells [14].

In this work, we have designed an improved version of p53_R peptide, called p53_H, by increasing its capabilities to both penetrate cancer cells and maintain the functional bioactive structure of p53 in its interaction with Mdm2. This is achieved by adding a cell penetrating sequence derived from penetratin, a linker and an apamin-inspired stretch of residues forcing covalent stabilization of the required alpha helical structure, without the need of non-natural stapling amino acids. By binding to MDM2 with nanomolar affinity, p53_H is designed to free p53 from its sequestrating complex allowing the induction of apoptosis. with the aim to compete in the binding and free p53 protein by disulfide bridges and added.
data.discussion:
Design of p53_H interfering peptide

The p53_H peptide was rationally designed by re-engineering the p53_R sequence to achieve robust covalent stabilization of its alpha-helical conformation. A fundamental design constraint was the exclusive use of canonical amino acids, thereby ensuring compatibility with in vivo biological synthesis. This strategic choice was made to enable future microbiome-based delivery approaches, wherein engineered commensal bacteria could be utilized to directly express and secrete the therapeutic peptide within the host.

To enforce this structural constraint, we employed an architectural motif inspired by apamin, a naturally occurring peptide that utilizes a highly rigid disulfide bridge network to lock its helical fold [15]. The apamin scaffold achieves this by pairing two extra-helical cysteines with two complementary cysteines positioned along one face of the alpha-helix, resulting in a tightly constrained covalent framework. Applying this structural logic, the MDM2-interacting interface of the p53 sequence was strictly conserved to preserve its binding affinity. Conversely, residues on the solvent-exposed, opposite face of the helix were mutated to cysteines to mimic the apamin topology. The complementary extra-helical apamin segment, required to mediate disulfide closure, was subsequently grafted onto the sequence.

To ensure intracellular bioavailability-a critical prerequisite for therapeutic efficacy-the cell-penetrating peptide (CPP) penetratin [16] was fused to the construct. To prevent structural cross-talk between the two functional domains, they were separated by a linker sequence incorporating a proline residue, which acts as a defined conformational breaker. This rational de novo design was iteratively evaluated in silico utilizing AlphaFold2 [17]. Sequential sequence optimizations were performed until the predicted three-dimensional fold faithfully matched the targeted, disulfide-constrained helical conformation.

The final sequence (RQIKIWFQNRRMKWKKSPQCNCKAPTSFACYWACLSP) was synthetised by solid phase forcing disulphide pairing.

p53_H assumes a covalently stabilized helical structure mimicking the Mdm2 binding conformation of p53

Figure 1A shows the structure of the transactivation domain of p53 interacting with Mdm2 (pdb code 1YCR [2]) compared with the crystal structure of the Mdm2 complex with the p53_R peptide (panel 1B, pdb code 3LNZ [13]) and with the alphafold structural prediction of the p53_H peptide (1C panel). The prediction of alpha helix in the highly charged N-terminal penetratin region of the peptide (shown in blue) is unlikely, as many repulsive charges would be kept close to each other. Indeed, AlphaFold classifies this region as highly uncertain. In contrast, the orange region-comprising 7 out of the 37 amino acids, or 19% of the total sequence-is expected to adopt an alpha-helical conformation.

To experimentally verify the presence of secondary structure elements, circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy was used (Figure 1D). Fitting the experimental spectrum by BeStSel web server [18] revealed a helical content of 22.5%, made up of 12.6% and 9.9% helical contributions. The undefined or disordered portion accounted for 44% of the signal, likely arising from the 16-residue cell-penetrating peptide segment at the N-terminus, which itself constitutes 43.2% of the full sequence. An additional 24.5% of the signal, consisting of 21.8% and 2.7%, corresponds to elongated or extended structures. These are probably associated with the CNCKAP motif adjacent to the predicted helix, which makes up 16% of the total residues, as well as with the terminal region of the cell-penetrating peptide segment. Finally, 9% of the signal is attributed to turn structures, which fits well with the SPQ motif, where the backbone folds back on itself; this motif comprises 8% of the sequence.

p53_H is effective against U2OS cancer cell and might display an improved therapeutic index

To evaluate the therapeutic potential of the p53_H peptide, we compared its anti-proliferative activity against the U2OS osteosarcoma cell line with that of p53_R and the standard chemotherapeutic agent doxorubicin, while also assessing its toxicity profile in the non-tumorigenic human embryonic kidney cell line HEK293 cell line. Cell viability assays (Figure 1E,F) demonstrated that p53_H exhibits significantly enhanced cytotoxicity compared to the control peptide p53_R. This may be attributed not only to the absence of helical stabilization in p53_R but also to the absence of the penetratin domain, which likely impairs its intracellular translocation.

Although the activity of p53_H remains lower than that of the DNA-intercalating agent doxorubicin, the peptide is distinguished by a significantly improved safety profile. The high sensitivity of U2OS cells to doxorubicin observed in our assay (IC₅₀ = 0.86 ± 0.67 μM) aligns with established pharmacological literature, which reports comparable sub-micromolar inhibitory concentrations for this cell line (0.69 ± 0.26 μM [19]). Furthermore, viability assays on healthy HEK293 cells reveal that p53_H induces comparable or less toxicity than Nutlin-a, a widely utilized non-genotoxic antagonist that serves as a benchmark for inhibiting the p53-MDM2 interaction. (34.46 ± 3.87 µM vs 8.08 ± 6.59 µM or 0.69 ± 0.26 µM according to the literature [20]) These findings suggest that the structural design of p53_H may achieve adequate anti-tumor efficacy while limiting off-target toxicity, thereby offering a more favorable therapeutic window.

p53_H Drives Low-Dose Apoptosis and High-Dose Catastrophic Clearance in U2OS Cells

To better understand the mechanism of action of p53_H, we performed multiparametric flow cytometry on U2OS cells following a 5-hour peptide exposure (Figure 2). Analysis of DAPI (Figure 2A) and Annexin V (Figure 2B) intensities revealed distinct apoptotic profiles. Data analysis demonstrated that p53_H is a highly potent cytotoxic agent against U2OS human osteosarcoma cells, exhibiting a biphasic mechanism of cell death dependent on the applied dose. At low concentrations (0.3 µM and 0.8 µM), p53_H effectively induces apoptosis in the U2OS cancer cells, as evidenced by the distinct high values of annexin compared to the controls and broadening of the Annexin V fluorescence peak. This early externalization of phosphatidylserine suggests that, at these precisely titrated low doses, p53_H successfully engages the intracellular apoptotic machinery, a biological response consistent with the intended therapeutic restoration of p53 function in this cancer model. As the concentration is escalated (> 2.5 µM), the lethality of p53_H becomes so rapid and severe that the U2OS cells undergo catastrophic fragmentation, resulting in an abrupt loss of intact events within the standard analytical gating (Figure 2A,B). This transition indicates that at higher doses, the compound's anti-cancer potency overwhelms the organized apoptotic machinery, driving cellular clearance or direct membrane disruption before late-stage markers can fully accumulate.

In comparison, the p53_R variant exhibits a much less potent, albeit classical, apoptotic profile in the U2OS cell line. p53_R drives a steady, dose-dependent progression of membrane permeabilization (DAPI, Figure 2C) and phosphatidylserine exposure (Annexin V, Figure 2D), achieving this physiological response requires significantly higher concentrations. In should be noted that the basal DAPI staining observed at the lowest p53_R concentrations reflects background permeabilization from the DMSO vehicle required for its formulation. Overall, p53_H demonstrates superior biological activity against U2OS cancer cells compared to p53_R, functioning as an inducer of apoptosis at sub-micromolar concentrations and an aggressive cytotoxic agent at elevated doses.

Live-cell time-lapse imaging shows that p53_H effectively penetrates into U2OS cell and, accumulates around the nucleus before exerting ts cytotoxic activity

To elucidate the cellular events leading up to the population clearance observed by flow cytometry, early time-lapse fluorescence microscopy was utilized to track the initial internalization and localization of the Alexa 488-conjugated p53_H construct in U2OS cells (Figure 3A). Facilitated by its penetratin sequence, the construct effectively breaches the cancer cell membrane, with intracellular accumulation starting to become clearly visible within 2 hours of incubation. Notably, by the 10-hour mark, the green p53_H signal is predominantly enriched in a distinct perinuclear pattern, tightly surrounding the nuclei rather than accumulating uniformly within the nucleoplasm. This cytoplasmic localization adjacent to the nucleus might reflect the continuous ubiquitin-dependent nuclear export of p53 mediated by the MDM2 E3 ubiquitin ligase [21,22]. Concurrently, the microscopic timeline captures the progressive induction of cytotoxicity. As the incubation progresses from 2 to 10 hours, an increasing number of cellular nuclei exhibit a distinct reddish fluorescence. This red signal-characteristic of membrane-impermeable dead-cell DNA dyes such as DRAQ7 entering cells with compromised plasma membranes-visually confirms that the successfully internalized p53_H construct actively kills the target cancer cells over time.

To better understand the flow cytometry results and investigate the abrupt loss of cellular events at higher concentrations, fluorescence microscopy was performed on U2OS cells after 24 hours of treatment. The untreated control panel displays a healthy, highly populated culture with a basal expression of p53 localized to the nucleus (Figure 3B). Following treatment with elevated concentrations of p53_H (10 µM and 50 µM), the imaging visually corroborates the high-dose clearance driven by the compound. The treatments induce a clear reduction in overall cell density compared to the untreated controls. While the sparse surviving cells maintain positive nuclear staining for p53, there is no widespread protein overexpression relative to the basal state. This confirms that the compound's cytotoxicity dominates the phenotype, effectively eradicating the bulk cancer cell population before massive intracellular accumulation of p53 can occur across the culture.

p53_H specifically interacts with MDM2 in vitro

While the ability of the compound to effectively induce apoptosis in tumor cells at low concentrations strongly implies that its mechanism of action is driven by the targeted engagement of MDM2, definitive biophysical validation is required. To provide conclusive evidence of this interaction, we monitored the binding of p53_H to ¹⁵N-enriched MDM2 in vitro using an NMR titration monitored by 2D ¹H-¹⁵N HSQC experiments (Figure 4A,B).

Upon stepwise addition of the peptide, the disappearance of the free-protein cross-peaks and the simultaneous emergence of a new set of signals were observed (Figure 4B). This spectral behavior indicates a binding event in the slow-exchange regime on the NMR timescale, which is a hallmark of high-affinity interactions and is consistent with the established affinity of the protein for this peptide [1,23].

To unambiguously demonstrate that the compound targets the intended binding site, we mapped the chemical shift perturbations (CSPs). Complete backbone reassignment of the protein in both its apo and peptide-bound states was performed using 3D HNCA and HNCACB experiments, leveraging established BMRB reference assignments (entries 15945 for the free protein [24] and 2410 for the bound form [25]). A comparative analysis of the free and complexed spectra allowed for the precise calculation of chemical shift perturbations CSPs (Figure 4C).

Strikingly, the most substantial spectral variations are strictly localized to the well-characterized binding pocket observed in X-ray crystallographic structures. The residues most affected by the interaction encompass Met50, Leu54, and Ile61 on the α2 helix; Leu66, Tyr67, His73, and Val93 on the central β-sheet; and Tyr100 on the α2' helix (Figure 4D)[2]. The perfect spatial correlation between the perturbed residues and the MDM2 canonical binding cleft provides unequivocal structural proof, definitively clarifying one key aspect of the mechanism of action of p53_H peptide.

data.conclusions:
Reactivating wild-type p53 by disrupting its inhibitory interaction with MDM2 represents a highly promising therapeutic strategy for p53-competent malignancies. In this study, we successfully engineered p53_H, a novel interfering peptide rationally designed to covalently stabilize the p53 transactivation domain in its bioactive alpha-helical conformation without relying on non-natural amino acids. By integrating a penetratin sequence with an apamin-inspired disulfide bridge architecture, p53_H overcomes traditional barriers of peptide therapeutics, achieving both efficient intracellular translocation and targeted perinuclear localization.

Our biophysical evaluations demonstrate that p53_H specifically engages the canonical MDM2 binding cleft, as unequivocally validated by NMR chemical shift perturbation mapping. Biologically, p53_H exhibits potent, dose-dependent anti-tumor activity in p53-wild-type U2OS cell lines. The peptide drives a distinct biphasic response: it triggers organized apoptosis at sub-micromolar concentrations while inducing catastrophic cellular clearance at elevated doses. Crucially, p53_H achieves this efficacy while maintaining a favorable safety profile and therapeutic window in healthy HEK293 cells, comparable or even improved to Nutlin-3.

To fully realize the therapeutic potential of p53_H, future investigations will focus on the downstream molecular cascade of p53 reactivation by confirming the transcriptional and translational upregulation of canonical apoptotic targets using RT-qPCR and western blot analyses. To bridge the gap between in vitro binding and in vivo efficacy, we plan to utilize in-cell NMR to directly monitor target engagement within the complex intracellular environment, complemented by studies of p53_H in its interaction with cancer cell membrane models. Ultimately, because the p53_H scaffold relies exclusively on canonical amino acids, this rational design paves the way for innovative, in-situ biological synthesis and microbiome-mediated delivery systems for next-generation cancer therapeutics.

materialsAndMethods.text:
U2OS cells were seeded in 96-well culture plates at a density of 5 × 10³ cells per well and incubated for 24 h to allow for adherence. Due to its limited aqueous solubility, the p53R peptide was solubilized in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), resulting in a maximum final DMSO concentration of 4% (v/v) in the assay medium. Cells were subsequently treated with p53H, p53R, or doxorubicin at a maximum initial compound concentration of 50 µM. The treatments were subjected to 10 progressive threefold serial dilutions, reaching a final minimum concentration of 0.001 µM. To account for any potential vehicle-induced cytotoxicity, vehicle control wells were treated with equivalent volumes of DMSO (matching the 4% v/v maximum). All viability experiments were conducted in biological triplicates.

Flow Cytometry and Apoptosis Analysis

U2OS cells were seeded in 96-well plates at a density of 1 × 10⁴ cells per well and allowed to adhere overnight. Treatments were administered directly in the 96-well plates at a maximum initial concentration of 200 µM, followed by six consecutive threefold serial dilutions to evaluate a 7-point concentration gradient terminating at 0.3 µM. Following this experimental layout, cells were incubated with the respective peptides and controls for 5 h. To ensure capture of the entire cell population, the culture medium containing non-adherent dead cells was collected. Adherent cells were harvested via trypsinization, quenched using the reserved culture medium, and pelleted by centrifugation.

For apoptosis quantification, the cell suspensions were sequentially stained with Tetramethylrhodamine, ethyl ester (TMRE) to assess mitochondrial membrane integrity, Allophycocyanin (APC)-conjugated Annexin V to detect externalized phosphatidylserine, and 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) to quantify dead cells. Staining was performed using standard incubation protocols at 37 °C and room temperature, protected from light. Flow cytometric data were acquired by gating for single cells (FSC-A vs. FSC-H) and excluding cellular debris (low FSC-A and SSC-A). Viable (low DAPI) and dead (high DAPI) populations were discriminated using DAPI vs. FSC-A plots, while apoptotic fractions were quantified using Annexin V vs. DAPI scatter plots.

To enable visualization by fluorescence microscopy, the p53_H and Myc_H peptides (100 µL of 100 µM solutions) were conjugated to Alexa Fluor® 488 using a commercially available conjugation kit. Reagents were equilibrated to room temperature (20-25°C) prior to use. For each peptide, 10 µL of Modifier reagent was added to the peptide solution and mixed gently. This mixture was directly applied to the lyophilized Alexa Fluor® 488 Conjugation Mix and resuspended by gentle pipetting. Following a 15-minute incubation in the dark at room temperature, 10 µL of Quencher reagent was added. The conjugate was ready for immediate use after a final 5-minute incubation.

For all microscopy experiments, U2OS cells were seeded at a density of 8,000 cells per well in 80 µL of complete culture medium (Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium [DMEM] supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum [FBS] and 1% penicillin/streptomycin). Cells were incubated overnight under standard conditions (37°C, 5% CO2) prior to imaging or staining procedures.

For live-cell tracking, the culture medium was replaced with 50 µL of serum- and antibiotic-free DMEM containing 5 ng/mL WGA-555 for 1 hour to label cellular membranes. Following a PBS wash, cells were incubated in 50 µL of complete DMEM containing Hoechst 33342 (0.5 ng/well) to label all nuclei and DRAQ7 (0.3 µM) to selectively label the nuclei of dead or permeabilized cells. After a 2-hour incubation, the cells were treated with the Alexa 488-conjugated peptides. For the 50 µM condition, 25 µL of medium was replaced with 25 µL of the 100 µM peptide stock; for the 5 µM condition, 2.5 µL of medium was replaced with 2.5 µL of the stock. Time-lapse imaging was initiated immediately, capturing images every 30 minutes over a 12-hour period.

Following cellular fixation, cells were permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100 in PBS for 5 minutes at room temperature, followed by three washes in PBS. Cells were then blocked in 3% Bovine Serum Albumin (BSA) in PBS for 30 minutes at room temperature.

Because both target primary antibodies for the p53 pathway were raised in mouse, they were applied in parallel to separate replicate wells to prevent cross-reactivity during secondary detection. Primary antibodies were diluted 1:200 in 3% BSA/PBS. Cells were incubated for 45 minutes at room temperature with 50 µL/well of either mouse anti-p53 (sc-126, Santa Cruz), mouse anti-MDM2 (sc-965, Santa Cruz), or a multiplex of rabbit anti-c-Myc (ab32072) and mouse anti-Max (sc-8011). To quantify non-specific secondary antibody binding and background fluorescence-particularly in dying or dead cells-negative control wells were incubated with 3% BSA/PBS lacking any primary antibody.

Following three PBS washes, cells were incubated for 45 minutes at room temperature with 50 µL/well of a secondary staining mixture containing anti-mouse Alexa Fluor 488 (2 µg/mL), anti-rabbit Alexa Fluor 555 (2 µg/mL), DAPI (1 µg/mL), and Cell Mask (5 µg/mL) diluted in PBS containing 0.3% BSA. All experimental and negative control wells received this secondary staining mixture. Finally, cells were washed three times in PBS and maintained in PBS for final fluorescence imaging.

MDM2 expression and purification

The DNA sequence codifying for MDM2 was used to transform E.coli BL21 (DE3) gold cells. A transformed colony was inoculated in 100 mL of 2xYT medium and incubated overnight at 310 K. An amount of cells corresponding to an initial OD600 of 0.1 in 1L of culture, was transferred into 1 L of M9 minimal medium supplemented with MgSO4 120 mg L-1,CaCl2 33 mg L-1, biotin 1 mg L-1, thiamine 1 mgL-1, ampicillin 100 mg L-1, 13C-labeled or unlabeled glucose 3 g L-1 and 15N-labeled or unlabeled ammonium sulfate 1.2 g L-1. Overexpression has been induced by the addition of 1 mM of IPTG at OD600 values between 0.6 and 0.8, and the solution was left incubating for 5 hours after induction. Cells pellet was resuspended in 20 mL/L of extracting buffer (50 mM tris-HCl, pH 8, 6 M GndCl, 8mM DTT) and left at 277 K under magnetic stirring O/N. The soluble fraction was collected, and the refolding has been induced dropping the protein into 300 mL/L of refolding buffer (50 mM tris-HCl, 500 mM NaCl, pH 8) and leaving the solution under magnetic stirring at 277 K for 10 minutes. The sample, than, has been loaded in a pre-equilibrated HisTrap FF 5 mL column with the binding buffer 50 mM tris-HCl, 500 mM NaCl, pH 8 and 5 mM Imidazole and eluted with 0-25% gradient of eluting buffer (50 mM tris-HCl, 500 mM NaCl, pH 8 and 500 mM Imidazole). The fractions containing the protein, checked with an SDS-Page gel, has been loaded in a size exclusion chromatography column (HiLoad Superdex 26/60 75pg) and eluted using a 50 mM KH2PO4 50 mM Na2HPO4 150 mM NaCl pH 7.5 buffer. To store the protein 5 mM DTT, 0.02% NaN3 and protease inhibitors have been added to the solution.

The NMR titration was performed to investigate the interaction between MDM2 and the peptide p53H through acquisition of 1H-15N HSQC spectra at 298 K at 900 MHz spectrometer. First, a reference spectrum of 15N-labeled 100 μM MDM2 in 50 mM KH2PO4 50 mM Na2HPO4 150 mM NaCl pH 7.5 was acquired. The titration was then performed by increasing the amount of p53H from 0.06 to 1.2 equivalents. The chemical shift changes observed by comparing the ¹H-¹⁵N HSQC spectra were reported as backbone-weighted average chemical shift differences, defined as Δδavg(HN) = (1/2)·[(ΔH)² + (ΔN/5)²]¹ᐟ², where ΔH and ΔN are the chemical shift differences between the free and bound protein for the backbone amide ¹H and ¹⁵N nuclei, respectively. The threshold used to identify meaningful chemical shift variations was estimated by calculating the average Δδavg(HN) value plus the standard deviation (σ).

Resonance assignments for both the free and complexed states were derived from previously deposited BMRB entries (15945 and 2410, respectively). Backbone chemical shifts were subsequently reassigned by acquiring 3D HNCA and HNCACB NMR spectra, with data analysis performed in CARA software.

data.discussion:
The interaction between MDM2 and p53H was investigated through an NMR titration, acquiring ¹H-¹⁵N HSQC experiments for each addition of increasing amounts of the peptide (Figure 1). The interaction between the two partners is in the slow-exchange regime on the NMR timescale, in agreement with the high affinity of the protein for the peptide (Figure 2), as reported in literature[1,2]. Spectral analysis was performed after chemical-shift reassignment of the protein, both in the free state and in the peptide-bound state, through the acquisition of the 3D HNCA and 3D HNCACB NMR experiments. The reassignment was carried out using reference assignments already available in the BMRB: 15945 was used for the free protein[3], and 2410 for the bound form[4]. The assignment data allowed the chemical shift perturbations (CSPs) calculation, by comparing the spectra of the free and complexed protein (Figure 3A). The residues most affected by the interaction are Met50, Leu54, and Ile61 from the α2 helix; Leu66, Tyr67, His73, and Val93 from the central β-sheet; and Tyr100 from the α2' helix[5] (Figure 3B).

materialsAndMethods.text:
MDM2 expression and purification

DNA sequences codifying for MDM2 was used to transform E.coli BL21 (DE3) gold cells. A transformed colony was inoculated in 100 mL of 2xYT medium and incubated overnight at 310 K. An amount of cells, corresponding to an initial OD600 of 0.1 in 1L of culture, was transferred into 1 L of M9 minimal medium supplemented with MgSO4 120 mg L-[1],CaCl2 33 mg L-1, biotin 1 mg L-1, thiamine 1 mgL-1, ampicillin 100 mg L-1, 13C-labeled or unlabeled glucose 3 g L-1, 15N-labeled or unlabeled ammonium sulfate 1.2 g L-1. The protein overexpression has been induced by the addition of 1 mM of IPTG when the OD600 reached a value between 0.6 and 0.8, and left incubating 5 hours after induction. Cells pellet was resuspended in 20 mL/L of extracting buffer (50 mM tris-HCl, pH 8, 6 M GndCl, 8mM DTT) and left at 277 K under magnetic stirring O/N. The soluble fraction was collected, and the refolding has been induced dropping the protein into 300 mL/L of refolding buffer (50 mM tris-HCl, 500 mM NaCl, pH 8) and leaving the solution under magnetic stirring at 277 K for 10 minutes. The sample, than, has been loaded in a pre-equilibrated HisTrap FF 5 mL column with the binding buffer 50 mM tris-HCl, 500 mM NaCl, pH 8 and 5 mM Imidazole and eluted with 0-25% gradient of eluting buffer (50 mM tris-HCl, 500 mM NaCl, pH 8 and 500 mM Imidazole). The fractions containing the protein, checked with an SDS-Page gel, has been loaded in a size exclusion chromatography column (HiLoad Superdex 26/60 75pg) and eluted using a 50 mM KH2PO4 50 mM Na2HPO4 150 mM NaCl pH 7.5 buffer. To store the protein 5 mM DTT, 0.02% NaN3 and protease inhibitors have been added to the solution.

The NMR titration was performed to investigate the interaction between MDM2 and the peptide p53H through acquisition of 1H-15N HSQC spectra at 298 K at 900 MHz spectrometer. First, a reference spectrum of 15N-labeled 100 μM MDM2 in 50 mM KH2PO4 50 mM Na2HPO4 150 mM NaCl pH 7.5 was acquired. The titration was then performed by increasing the amount of p53H from 0.06 to 1.2 equivalents. The chemical shift changes observed by comparing the ¹H-¹⁵N HSQC spectra were reported as backbone-weighted average chemical shift differences, defined as Δδavg(HN) = (1/2)·[(ΔH)² + (ΔN/5)²]¹ᐟ², where ΔH and ΔN are the chemical shift differences between the free and bound protein for the backbone amide ¹H and ¹⁵N nuclei, respectively. The threshold used to identify meaningful chemical shift variations was estimated by calculating the average Δδavg(HN) value plus the standard deviation (σ).

The reassignment of both the free and the complexed protein was performed using assignments already deposited in the BMRB: entry 15945 was used for the free protein, and entry 2410 for the complexed form. The 3D HNCA and HNCACB NMR experiments were recorded to reassign the backbone chemical shifts, and the analysis was carried out using the CARA software.
